texto:
Amazon on November 6, 2026 began letting a small, invitation-only group of US customers shop by text message with Alexa for Shopping, the AI assistant it formed in May by merging Rufus and Alexa+. Invited customers accept terms, link a phone number and then message a contact that appears on their phone as "Alexa Shopping," which searches for products, compares them, builds carts, completes purchases and sends delivery updates, according to Amazon. The company said the option will reach millions more customers in the coming weeks. It gave no size for the first group, did not name the messaging technology involved and said nothing about whether advertising will appear in the conversations.
In Short
Amazon now lets some people in the US send a text message to its AI shopping helper, which can find products, fill a cart and buy things for them without anyone opening the Amazon app. That matters to brands and sellers because a text reply has room for only a few products, so whichever items Amazon's system mentions get almost all the attention, and Amazon has not said how ads will work there. More people are due to get the option over the coming weeks, which runs straight into the holiday shopping peak.
How the text option works
The announcement, published on Amazon's news site and written by Jacquelyn Smith, describes a staged rollout. "Beginning today, a subset of U.S. customers will receive a text message inviting them to try the experience," the post says, dated November 6. To start, a customer accepts the terms, links a phone number and begins messaging. Customers who have not been invited can register on a landing page at amazon.com/text-alexa-shopping. That page, according to Amazon, signs them up "to get news and offers from Amazon by text," and those customers "will be among the first to know when more invites are sent."
The waitlist, in other words, doubles as a sign-up for Amazon's marketing texts. The post does not say whether a customer can join the queue for the assistant without also agreeing to receive offers.
Amazon describes the scale of the expansion in three slightly different ways in the same document. The subheading says the option is "rolling out to customers across the U.S. in the coming weeks." The key takeaways speak of "a small group of U.S. customers by invitation only, with the option expanding to more customers over the coming weeks." The body says it "will roll out to millions more customers in the coming weeks." None of the three gives a date for general availability, and none gives a number for the group invited on day one.
Amazon framed the channel around an existing habit. "Customers often jot down what they need the moment they think of it in their notes, in their messages, in their group chats," said Rajiv Mehta, vice president of Conversational Shopping at Amazon. "Now with Alexa for Shopping, your personal shopping agent is just a text away. Message it what you need, and Alexa goes to work on your behalf - searching, comparing, and buying so you can get on with your day."
On the phone, the assistant appears as a contact named "Alexa Shopping." Amazon did not say whether the service runs over SMS, RCS or Apple's iMessage, whether standard carrier messaging rates apply, or whether a Prime membership is required. Alexa for Shopping itself has required no Prime membership for its core features since it launched on May 13, 2026 on the Amazon Shopping app, the Amazon website and Echo Show devices. That launch did not mention text messaging.
What a text can do
Most of what Amazon lists for the text channel already exists inside the app. What changes is the entry point. The post gives twelve categories of request, each with an example phrased the way a customer might type it.
Several combine more than one task. A single text reading "I'm out of dog food, need a birthday gift for my sister, and we're low on paper towels" sets the assistant working on all three, "messaging back with product suggestions as it finds them," according to Amazon. Grocery requests can set up a weekly order, turn a photo of a recipe into a cart, or ask for delivery against a clock: the example given is "deliver eggs, bacon, pancake mix, and maple syrup in 30 minutes." That example falls squarely within quick commerce, although Amazon did not say in which areas a 30-minute window is available. Orders can be amended by message ("add broccoli to my last order"), and the assistant can suggest dinner ideas based on recent purchases.
The remaining categories map onto features Amazon has added to its assistant since 2025:
- Reorders, with the example "reorder the laundry detergent I bought last month."
- Standing preferences, such as "add items to my cart automatically," "only show me organic options" or "give me nutritional information whenever I ask about food."
- Photos, which the assistant uses to find similar products on Amazon. Camera search has been tied to the assistant since Lens Live launched on September 2, 2025, with Rufus suggesting questions beneath the matches.
- Deal and price tracking, with the example "let me know when AirPods go on sale."
- List management, including grocery lists and a new holiday gift list.
- Order status, where a text asking "where's my package?" returns an update "without opening the app."
- Products from other stores, which Amazon surfaces through Shop Direct.
- New-release alerts, such as "update me when Nike drops new running shoes," which Amazon says monitors "Amazon and the broader web."
- Comparisons, such as "compare the top-rated robot vacuums," drawing on key details, reviews and pricing.
- Price history, showing "up to a full year of pricing" for a product.
The announcement also links to a separate Amazon post headlined "Alexa for Shopping adds 100+ new capabilities to make shopping even faster and easier," which covers holiday gift lists, baby registries and refund tracking. The text announcement does not say when those capabilities arrived, or how many of them work by text.
How much the assistant does without asking
The post is not consistent about when a purchase needs the customer's say-so. The reorder example states that Alexa for Shopping "finds it and buys it with your approval." Elsewhere, the assistant "can add items to your cart and seamlessly complete the purchase on your behalf" once the customer is ready, and customers can instruct it to add items to their cart automatically. Auto-buy, which Amazon describes in the same post, will "complete a purchase when the price is right."
Those are different levels of autonomy, and the document does not explain how approval is given in a text thread: whether a reply such as "yes" is enough, whether a code or a link to the app is required, or how Amazon confirms that a message comes from the account holder. Linking a phone number is the only setup step described.
One thread across the app, the website and Echo
Amazon is also connecting the text channel to the assistant's other surfaces. According to the post, Amazon is "rolling out the ability for a request started over text to carry over to Alexa for Shopping in the Amazon Shopping app, on Amazon.com, and on Alexa-enabled devices, and vice versa." The wording describes a rollout in progress rather than a finished feature.
The memory behind that continuity predates the text option. In November 2025, Rufus gained memory, price tracking and auto-buying. By April 2026, a "Tell us about you" prompt in Rufus was saving persistent shopper profiles, and PPC Land noted at the time that Amazon had not disclosed retention periods or whether the profile data fed ad targeting. The May launch of Alexa for Shopping listed stored attributes such as family members, pets, interests and dietary needs.
The text post adds two examples of that memory at work. "Tell it you only want to see vegan products, and it remembers," Amazon writes, and a customer who mentions marathon training will find "it factors that into future recommendations." This is hyper-personalization carried into a messaging app. The post does not say how long text conversations, or the photos customers send, are retained, or whether they can be deleted separately from other Alexa data.
The thread will also carry more than conversation. "Over time, your Alexa Shopping contact will also include your Amazon order updates, delivery notifications, and deals - all in the same thread as your shopping conversations," according to Amazon. Order updates are service messages. Deals are promotions. Amazon did not say how the deals in the thread will be selected, how often they will arrive, or whether brands will be able to pay to appear among them.
The numbers Amazon gave
The post repeats a figure Amazon chief executive Andy Jassy gave on October 29: more than 400 million customers have used Alexa for Shopping in the last 12 months. On that earnings call, Jassy also said US customers who use the assistant spend 50% more per order than those who do not, and that customer interactions had risen 570% year over year.
One figure is new. "The number of customers using Alexa for Shopping's agentic features has grown more than eight times since the start of the year," Amazon says. It gives no starting count, does not list which features it counts as agentic, and does not say whether the measure covers US customers only. Without a base, an eightfold rise could describe a large audience or a small one. The figure also measures something different from the 570% growth in interactions: one counts people since January, the other counts exchanges against a year earlier.
Amazon does not define "agentic" anywhere in the post. The functions it describes as acting on a customer's behalf include buying at a target price, monitoring prices and new releases, automating recurring orders and completing purchases on other sites. That is the territory of agentic AI, and it is where Amazon has concentrated its recent changes. In November 2025, the company said its Buy for Me agent, which completes purchases on other retailers' websites, had grown from 65,000 products at launch to more than half a million.
The post also calls Alexa for Shopping "the best personal AI agent for shopping." Amazon offers no comparison or test to support that description.
Shop Direct comes along
The text channel extends the reach of a programme Amazon has been building for outside merchants. On March 11, 2026, Amazon opened Shop Direct to third-party feeds through Feedonomics, Salsify and CEDCommerce, and said the programme included more than 100 million products from more than 400,000 merchants. Two days before the text announcement, on November 4, it launched a free self-service portal through which eligible US stores can list products in Amazon search and in Alexa for Shopping without selling on Amazon. Amazon gave no merchant count or traffic figures for that portal.
The text post confirms that the assistant "can surface options from stores across the web through Shop Direct" in a text conversation. It does not say how products from outside stores are ranked against items sold on Amazon in a reply that may name only a handful of options, or whether merchants will see which sales began in a text thread.
Messaging becomes a shopping surface
Amazon is not the first company to put a buying agent where people already send messages. On September 8, 2026, Meta released Muse, which people can use in a dedicated app or directly in WhatsApp, with an agent that can buy things for US users. On September 20, Amazon said it had cut Muse off from buying on Amazon.com after Meta declined to leave Amazon out, objecting among other things that the agent did not identify itself. Jassy told analysts on October 29 that Amazon expects Alexa for Shopping to be the primary agent customers use to shop Amazon, even as it anticipates working with general-purpose agents built by others.
Walmart has taken a different route for its own assistant. Its October 30 update gave Sparky the ability to turn photos of handwritten lists into carts, along with image input and recipe planning, inside Walmart's app; voice was expected chainwide by the end of the year. Nine days earlier, Walmart had set out rules for outside AI agents, including customer-set spending limits of $50, $100 or $200.
Google's shopping tools have so far used text messages to deliver results rather than to take orders. Its agentic checkout, launched on November 13, 2025, let US users have Google buy a tracked product from an eligible merchant once it met their budget, with explicit confirmation required, while its store-calling feature returned results by email or text. On the advertising side, messaging threads have been opening up as a channel in their own right: on October 28, Invoca released AI agents, in beta, that hold conversations started from Google Search over Google's RCS for Business channel. The same day, a Google Search ad was posted on X with an Apple Messages button that opened a pre-filled SMS on iPhone, a button Google had not announced.
Why would Amazon move its assistant into the text inbox when it already has a shopping app? Its post does not say, beyond convenience. Survey data offers one possible reason. In an August survey of 1,000 US consumers, Adobe found that 72% had installed a retail app for a single discount or purchase and then deleted it, and that order tracking was the AI feature most likely to keep an app on a phone, cited by 65%. A messaging contact needs no install and no storage, and Amazon's own example of the order-status query stresses that it works "without opening the app."
Why it matters for marketers
For brands that sell on Amazon, the shelf keeps getting shorter. A results page in the app shows dozens of products and several sponsored slots. Research by Workflow Labs published in April found that Rufus narrowed discovery from 50 results to roughly five named products. A text message, read on a lock screen, has less room still. Which products the assistant names in a reply becomes the decision that matters, and Amazon has said nothing about how that choice is made in this channel.
Amazon already sells placements inside the assistant. Sponsored Products and Sponsored Brands prompts launched as a free beta in November 2025 and became billable on March 25, 2026 in the United States under existing cost-per-click bids. If those prompts reach text threads, advertisers would be paying for a format they cannot see in the same way as a results page. If they do not, a growing share of assistant shopping could take place in a channel where Amazon's retail media network has no visible inventory, apart from whatever deals Amazon chooses to send.
The thread is also a direct line from Amazon to the customer. Once order updates, delivery notifications and deals sit in one conversation, Amazon controls a messaging channel built on phone numbers customers have linked to their accounts, and the waitlist adds more of them. Brands that rely on their own SMS programmes for reorders and promotions would be competing with a contact that already knows the customer's purchase history, address and payment details.
Timing adds pressure. Black Friday falls on November 27, 2026, three weeks after the first invitations. A rollout "in the coming weeks" places the text channel in front of millions of customers during the busiest shopping period of the year, before Amazon has published how it ranks products, how approvals work or where advertising fits.

Summary
Who: Amazon, which runs the Alexa for Shopping assistant, and Rajiv Mehta, its vice president of Conversational Shopping; US customers invited to the text option; brands, sellers and Shop Direct merchants whose products appear in the assistant's replies.
What: Amazon began letting invited US customers shop with Alexa for Shopping by text message, through a phone contact named "Alexa Shopping" that searches, compares, builds carts, completes purchases, tracks prices and sends order updates. Requests started by text are to carry over to the app, the website and Alexa devices, and the thread will later include order updates, delivery notifications and deals. Amazon said users of the assistant's agentic features have grown more than eightfold since the start of the year, without giving a base. It did not say whether ads will appear in text replies.
When: The first invitations went out on November 6, 2026. Amazon said millions more customers will get the option in the coming weeks, a period that includes Black Friday on November 27, 2026.
Where: The United States only. Customers who have not been invited can register at amazon.com/text-alexa-shopping, a sign-up that also enrols them for Amazon news and offers by text.
Why: Amazon wants its own assistant to be where customers shop, and a messaging contact reaches people without an app being opened. For advertisers, a text reply shows only a few products, and Amazon has not explained how those products are chosen, whether sponsored placements will appear, or how purchases are approved.
